module.title: Proofs
module.description: Module 3 introduces the machinery of formal proof: rules of inference for propositional and predicate logic (Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Hypothetical Syllogism, Disjunctive Syllogism, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, Resolution, plus UI, UG, EI, EG); the cornerstone proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, vacuous, trivial); biconditional proofs; and advanced strategies including proof by cases, without loss of generality, constructive vs nonconstructive existence, counterexamples, uniqueness, and forward vs backward reasoning. By the end of this module a student can read and write formal proofs in the style used throughout the rest of the course.

lessons.title: Rules of Inference
lessons.welcome: Welcome to Module 3. In Modules 1 and 2 you built precise statements; now it is time to BUILD ARGUMENTS that go from given premises to a justified conclusion. The atoms of mechanical reasoning are RULES OF INFERENCE — small, named patterns that every formal proof, every verified-software tool, and every automated theorem prover relies on. Master these and you can certify your reasoning instead of merely hoping it is right.
objectives: Define a valid argument and explain why valid arguments are tautologies in implication form.
Apply the standard inference rules: Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Hypothetical Syllogism, Disjunctive Syllogism, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, and Resolution.
Use the four quantifier rules — Universal Instantiation, Universal Generalization, Existential Instantiation, Existential Generalization.
Chain inference rules together to produce a multi-step formal proof from premises.
Recognize and avoid common fallacies, especially affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: Why can't I just check arguments with a truth table?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: You can — for tiny cases. But truth tables grow exponentially: ten propositional variables means 1024 rows. Inference rules let you build a proof in a number of steps that scales linearly with the argument's complexity.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: An argument is valid when, whenever every premise is true, the conclusion is also true. Equivalently, the conjunction of premises implies the conclusion as a tautology. Validity is about the SHAPE of the argument, not whether the premises are actually true.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: And the rules — like Modus Ponens — are just small valid argument forms?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Exactly. Each rule is a tiny tautology. Chain enough of them together and you can prove arbitrarily complex theorems.

sections.heading: Valid Arguments and Argument Forms
sections.explanation:
An ARGUMENT in propositional logic is a sequence of propositions p₁, p₂, …, pₙ called PREMISES, followed by a final proposition q called the CONCLUSION. The argument is VALID if whenever every premise is true, the conclusion is also true. Equivalently, the implication

  (p₁ ∧ p₂ ∧ ⋯ ∧ pₙ) → q

must be a tautology. An ARGUMENT FORM is the abstract pattern of an argument, written with propositional variables. A form is valid if it is valid no matter what concrete propositions you substitute for its variables.
examples: Premises: 'If it rains, the road is wet.' 'It is raining.' Conclusion: 'The road is wet.' This is the valid form p → q, p ⊢ q.

Validity is about FORM, not content. If we substitute 'I am the king of England' and 'I have a crown' for p and q, the same form still produces a valid argument — even if the premises happen to be false.
common_mistakes: Conflating validity with soundness. A SOUND argument is valid AND has all true premises. Validity alone says nothing about whether the premises are actually true.
Believing one example proves an argument valid. Validity is universal across substitutions — only argument forms can be valid.

visual_idea.description: A horizontal line separating the premises (above) from the conclusion (below). Below the line, a small checkmark turns green if every row of the truth table has 'all premises true ⇒ conclusion true', and red otherwise.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Toggle each premise's truth value; the diagram highlights any row where premises are true but the conclusion is false — those rows kill validity.

sections.heading: The Eight Standard Rules of Inference
sections.explanation:
Memorize these eight rules. Each is named, each is a tautology in implication form, and each can be applied instantly when you spot its pattern.

  Modus Ponens (MP)         [p, p → q] ⊢ q
  Modus Tollens (MT)        [¬q, p → q] ⊢ ¬p
  Hypothetical Syllogism    [p → q, q → r] ⊢ p → r
  Disjunctive Syllogism     [p ∨ q, ¬p] ⊢ q
  Addition                  [p] ⊢ p ∨ q
  Simplification            [p ∧ q] ⊢ p
  Conjunction               [p, q] ⊢ p ∧ q
  Resolution                [p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r] ⊢ q ∨ r

MP and MT are by far the most-used. Resolution is the engine of automated theorem provers. Addition and Simplification look almost trivial but show up constantly as 'glue' inside larger derivations.
examples: MP: from 'If you study, you pass' and 'You study', conclude 'You pass'.
MT: from 'If it snows, the school closes' and 'The school is open', conclude 'It is not snowing'.
DS: from 'It is raining or sunny' and 'It is not raining', conclude 'It is sunny'.
Resolution: from 'p ∨ q' and '¬p ∨ r', conclude 'q ∨ r'.
common_mistakes: Affirming the Consequent: from p → q and q, INVALIDLY concluding p. This looks like MP but is not.
Denying the Antecedent: from p → q and ¬p, INVALIDLY concluding ¬q. This looks like MT but is not.

visual_idea.description: A reference card with two columns: rule name and premise→conclusion pattern. Color-code by rule family: MP/MT (yellow), HS/DS (blue), Addition/Simplification/Conjunction (green), Resolution (purple).
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click a rule to see one worked English example and one symbolic example.

sections.heading: Building a Multi-Step Proof
sections.explanation:
A FORMAL PROOF is a numbered sequence of propositions. The first lines are the premises; each subsequent line is either another premise or a result derived from earlier lines using a named rule (or a logical equivalence from Module 1). The last line is the conclusion. Each line must cite the rule and the line numbers it depended on.

Proof discipline:
  1. Number each line.
  2. Justify each non-premise line with a rule name + line numbers.
  3. Stop when you reach the conclusion.
examples:
Premises: ¬p ∨ ¬f → (s ∧ d), s → t, ¬t. Goal: r (where p, f, r combine into the larger context). 1. ¬p ∨ ¬f → (s ∧ d)   premise
2. s → t                premise
3. ¬t                   premise
4. ¬s                   MT (2, 3)
5. ¬s ∨ ¬d              Addition (4)
6. ¬(s ∧ d)             De Morgan (5)
7. ¬(¬p ∨ ¬f)           MT (1, 6)
8. p ∧ f                De Morgan + double negation (7)
common_mistakes: Skipping justifications. A line without a rule citation is not part of a proof.
Using a rule out of pattern. Always verify the premises for the rule actually appear on earlier lines.

visual_idea.description: A 'proof tree builder' shaped like a directed acyclic graph: each node is a line of the proof, edges flow from premises to derived results, and edges are labeled with the rule applied.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Drag two premise nodes onto a rule symbol; the page creates a new node with the inferred result and links it back. Wrong combinations show a 'pattern mismatch' error.

sections.heading: Inference Rules for Quantifiers
sections.explanation:
Predicate-logic proofs add four quantifier rules.

  Universal Instantiation (UI)
       ∀x P(x)            ⊢  P(c)   for any specific c.

  Universal Generalization (UG)
       P(c) for an ARBITRARY c   ⊢  ∀x P(x).
       (c must have been introduced as 'arbitrary', not named)

  Existential Instantiation (EI)
       ∃x P(x)            ⊢  P(c) for SOME FRESH c not used elsewhere.

  Existential Generalization (EG)
       P(c)               ⊢  ∃x P(x).

Strategy: from a universal premise, INSTANTIATE to a specific element (UI). From an existential premise, name a FRESH witness (EI). Combine with propositional rules. Finally GENERALIZE back to ∀ or ∃ as the goal demands.
examples: From ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) and P(a): UI gives P(a) → Q(a); MP with P(a) gives Q(a).
From ∃x P(x): EI introduces a fresh constant c with P(c). The c is a witness whose specific identity is unknown.
From P(a): EG gives ∃x P(x).
common_mistakes: Reusing an existing name in EI. The witness from ∃x P(x) must be a NEW constant.
Applying UG to a non-arbitrary element. UG requires that the element was introduced as 'arbitrary', not as a specific named instance.
Forgetting to instantiate before applying propositional rules.

visual_idea.description: Four labeled cards arranged in a square, one per quantifier rule. Each card shows the input pattern on top, an arrow, and the output pattern below. The UI/EI side is colored 'instantiate'; the UG/EG side is colored 'generalize'.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Drag a quantified statement onto a UI/EI card to see the instantiated form; drag an instance onto UG/EG to generalize. Invalid moves (e.g., UG on a named element) show a red banner.

sections.heading: Common Fallacies
sections.explanation:
Two patterns LOOK like inference rules but are NOT. Avoiding them is half the battle.

  AFFIRMING THE CONSEQUENT — INVALID:
       from p → q and q, conclude p.
  Counterexample: 'If it rains the road is wet. The road is wet. Therefore it is raining.' But the road might be wet from a sprinkler.

  DENYING THE ANTECEDENT — INVALID:
       from p → q and ¬p, conclude ¬q.
  Counterexample: 'If it rains the road is wet. It is not raining. Therefore the road is not wet.' Again, the sprinkler.

Whenever you see an implication and one of its parts, check carefully whether the rule you want is MP, MT, or neither.
examples: VALID (MT): 'If you study you pass. You did not pass. Therefore you did not study.'
INVALID (denying the antecedent): 'If you study you pass. You did not study. Therefore you did not pass.' — you might still pass without studying.
common_mistakes: Treating the converse of an implication as if it followed from the original.
Treating the inverse of an implication as if it followed from the original.

visual_idea.description: Four-row table: MP (valid), MT (valid), Affirming the Consequent (invalid), Denying the Antecedent (invalid). Each row shows the pattern in symbols and a one-line English example. The two invalid rows are shaded red.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click any row to see a counterexample for the invalid patterns or a tautology check for the valid ones.

worked_examples.problem: Premises: (1) 'If it does not rain or if it is not foggy, then the sailing race will be held and the lifesaving demonstration will go on.' (2) 'If the sailing race is held, then the trophy will be awarded.' (3) 'The trophy was not awarded.' Show: it rained.
step_by_step_solution: Let r = it rained, f = foggy, s = sailing race held, d = lifesaving demonstration, t = trophy awarded.
1. (¬r ∨ ¬f) → (s ∧ d)   premise
2. s → t                  premise
3. ¬t                     premise
5. ¬s ∨ ¬d                Addition (4)
6. ¬(s ∧ d)               De Morgan (5)
8. r ∧ f                  De Morgan + double negation (7)
9. r                      Simplification (8)
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each step uses a single rule on previously established lines. Modus Tollens twice (lines 4 and 7) drives the argument; Addition and De Morgan are the connective glue.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to prove r directly from premise 1 without first establishing ¬(s ∧ d). Without that intermediate result, MT cannot be applied to premise 1.

worked_examples.problem: Show: from ∀x (P(x) → (Q(x) ∧ S(x))) and ∀x (P(x) ∧ R(x)), conclude ∀x (R(x) ∧ S(x)).
step_by_step_solution: Let c be an ARBITRARY element of the domain.
1. P(c) ∧ R(c)              UI on second premise
2. P(c)                     Simplification (1)
3. R(c)                     Simplification (1)
4. P(c) → Q(c) ∧ S(c)       UI on first premise
6. S(c)                     Simplification (5)
7. R(c) ∧ S(c)              Conjunction (3, 6)
worked_examples.why_it_works: UI brings the universals down to a specific (but arbitrary) element c; propositional rules combine the facts; UG promotes the result back to a universal.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to introduce c as 'arbitrary'. Without that, UG at the end is invalid — the result would only apply to the specific element you chose.

worked_examples.problem: Identify the rule used: 'If it snows today, the university will close. The university is not closed today. Therefore it did not snow today.'
step_by_step_solution: Let p = 'it snows today', q = 'the university closes'.
Premise 1: p → q. Premise 2: ¬q. Conclusion: ¬p.
Pattern: ¬q, p → q ⊢ ¬p.
This is exactly Modus Tollens.
worked_examples.why_it_works: MT lets you reject the antecedent of an implication once you know the consequent fails.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Mistaking this for denying the antecedent. The given argument denies the CONSEQUENT (¬q), not the antecedent.

quick_checks.question: From premises 'If I study, I pass' and 'I do not pass', conclude:
quick_checks.explanation: Modus Tollens: from p → q and ¬q, conclude ¬p.

quick_checks.question: From p ∨ q and ¬p ∨ r, Resolution yields:
quick_checks.explanation: Resolution cancels p with ¬p and disjoins the remaining literals.

quick_checks.question: From p → q and q, you can validly conclude p.
quick_checks.explanation: That is the fallacy of affirming the consequent. There may be other reasons q holds.

key_takeaways: An argument is valid when every truth assignment that makes the premises true also makes the conclusion true.
Eight standard rules: Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Hypothetical Syllogism, Disjunctive Syllogism, Addition, Simplification, Conjunction, Resolution.
Quantifier rules: UI, UG, EI, EG. Always introduce a FRESH constant when applying EI; always introduce an ARBITRARY element when applying UG.
Affirming the consequent and denying the antecedent are common fallacies — they look like MP/MT but are not.
A formal proof is a numbered sequence of justified lines, ending at the conclusion.
summary.next: Next we move from individual inference steps to PROOF METHODS — direct, contrapositive, contradiction, vacuous, and trivial — that organize an entire argument from hypothesis to conclusion.

lessons.title: Introduction to Proofs
lessons.welcome: Inference rules are the alphabet; PROOFS are the literature. A proof transforms a conjecture — something you suspect — into a theorem — something you and every future reader can rely on. In this lesson you will learn the vocabulary of mathematical writing, the four cornerstone proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, vacuous/trivial), and how to prove biconditional statements.
objectives: Distinguish theorem, axiom, lemma, corollary, conjecture, and proof.
Produce a direct proof of an implication p → q.
Produce a proof by contraposition (¬q → ¬p) when direct proof is awkward.
Produce a proof by contradiction by assuming the negation of the claim and deriving a contradiction.
Recognize trivial proofs (q is true) and vacuous proofs (p is false), and prove biconditional statements as two implications.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: How do I prove 'if n is odd, then n² is odd'?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Direct proof. Assume the hypothesis: n is odd, so n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. Square it: n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1 — that has the form 2r + 1, so n² is odd.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: What about the converse: if n² is odd, then n is odd?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Direct is awkward — you would have to factor an odd square. Try CONTRAPOSITION: assume n is even, show n² is even. n = 2k, so n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), even. Done.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: That is a classic CONTRADICTION proof. Assume √2 = a/b in lowest terms; derive that a and b are both even — contradicting 'lowest terms'.

sections.heading: The Vocabulary of Mathematical Writing
sections.explanation:
Before writing proofs, learn the words mathematicians use:

  THEOREM — a claim that has been proven true.
  AXIOM (postulate) — a foundational truth taken without proof.
  LEMMA — a 'helper' theorem used inside a larger proof.
  COROLLARY — an immediate consequence of a theorem.
  CONJECTURE — a statement believed true but unproven.
  PROOF — a finite sequence of statements, each justified by an axiom, definition, previously proven theorem, or rule of inference, ending with the desired claim.

And four definitions you will use constantly in Module 3 examples:
  • n is EVEN iff there exists an integer k with n = 2k.
  • n is ODD iff there exists an integer k with n = 2k + 1.
  • r is RATIONAL iff there exist integers p, q with q ≠ 0 and r = p/q.
  • A real that is not rational is IRRATIONAL.
examples: Theorem: 'For every integer n, if n is odd, then n² is odd.'
Lemma (used inside a bigger proof): 'The product of two even integers is even.'
Corollary: 'The sum of three even integers is even' follows immediately from 'sum of two evens is even'.
Conjecture: 'Every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes' (Goldbach — still unproven).
common_mistakes: Calling any helpful side-result a 'theorem'. Reserve the word 'theorem' for the central, named claim. Helper results are lemmas.
Treating a conjecture as a fact in a proof. Conjectures are unproven and cannot be cited as justification.

visual_idea.description: A pyramid: AXIOMS at the base, LEMMAS in the middle, THEOREMS near the top, COROLLARIES branching off theorems. CONJECTURES float beside the pyramid, labeled 'unproven' until promoted.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click any tier to see one example claim from discrete math at that level.

sections.heading: Direct Proof
sections.explanation:
To prove p → q DIRECTLY: assume p is true, then use definitions, axioms, previously proven theorems, and logical rules to derive q. The skeleton is:

  1. 'Assume p.'
  2. (chain of justified deductions)
  3. 'Therefore q. ∎'

Direct proof is the FIRST method to try. It is usually the cleanest and most informative when it works.
examples: Theorem: 'The sum of two even integers is even.' Proof: let m = 2a, n = 2b. m + n = 2(a + b), an integer multiple of 2. ∎
Theorem: 'Every odd integer is the difference of two squares.' Proof: let n = 2k + 1. Then (k + 1)² − k² = 2k + 1 = n. ∎
common_mistakes: Assuming the conclusion. The conclusion q is what you are trying to derive — not what you start with.
Skipping the 'why'. Each step should cite a definition, theorem, or rule.

visual_idea.description: A vertical chain: 'Assume p' at the top, intermediate boxes for each derivation step (each labelled with the definition or rule used), 'Therefore q' at the bottom. The chain is highlighted green to signify a valid direct path.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click a step to expand it — show the definition or previously proven result the step depends on.

sections.heading: Proof by Contraposition
sections.explanation:
Recall p → q is logically equivalent to its contrapositive ¬q → ¬p. Sometimes the contrapositive is easier to prove directly than the original.

  Skeleton:
  1. 'We prove the contrapositive: ¬q → ¬p.'
  2. 'Assume ¬q.'
  3. (derive ¬p)
  4. 'Therefore by contraposition, p → q. ∎'

When to reach for contraposition: when the hypothesis p is hard to manipulate (e.g., 'n² is odd') but ¬q is easy to manipulate (e.g., 'n is even').
examples: Theorem: 'For integer n, if n² is odd, then n is odd.' Direct attempt is messy. Contrapositive: assume n is even, n = 2k. Then n² = 4k² = 2(2k²), even. ∎
Theorem: 'If x + y ≥ 2 (real x, y), then x ≥ 1 or y ≥ 1.' Contrapositive: assume x < 1 AND y < 1. Then x + y < 2. ∎
common_mistakes: Confusing contrapositive with converse. The converse is q → p — NOT equivalent.
Forgetting to negate BOTH parts when forming ¬q → ¬p.

visual_idea.description: A four-cell square with the original p → q on the top-left and the contrapositive ¬q → ¬p on the bottom-right, connected by a green double-arrow labeled 'logically equivalent'. The other two cells (converse and inverse) are connected by a red dashed arrow labeled 'NOT equivalent to original'.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Type any implication and the diagram fills the four cells with its converse, contrapositive, and inverse automatically.

sections.heading: Proof by Contradiction (Reductio ad Absurdum)
sections.explanation:
To prove a claim p by CONTRADICTION: assume ¬p and derive a contradiction (something of the form r ∧ ¬r). Since ¬p leads to absurdity, ¬p must be false, so p is true. This method is especially powerful when proving NEGATIVE claims (e.g., 'no integer satisfies …') or claims about infinity.

  Skeleton:
  1. 'Suppose for contradiction that ¬p.'
  2. (derive a contradiction)
  3. 'This is impossible. Therefore p. ∎'

For an implication p → q, assume p ∧ ¬q and derive any contradiction.
examples: Theorem: '√2 is irrational.' Suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms. Then 2b² = a², so a is even, say a = 2c. Then 2b² = 4c², so b² = 2c², so b is even. But a, b being both even contradicts 'lowest terms'. ∎

Theorem: 'There are infinitely many primes.' Suppose there are only finitely many: p₁, …, pₙ. Form r = p₁p₂⋯pₙ + 1. r leaves remainder 1 when divided by any pᵢ, so either r is a new prime or has a prime factor not in the list — contradicting the assumption of completeness. ∎
common_mistakes: Deriving a small inconsistency that is not actually a contradiction. The contradiction must be of the form r ∧ ¬r — both r and its negation must follow from the assumption.
Forgetting to negate the original claim. To prove p, you assume ¬p — not p itself.

visual_idea.description: A diamond marked 'Assume ¬p'; below it, a chain of deductions; at the bottom, two boxes labelled r and ¬r colliding into a red 'CONTRADICTION' explosion. An arrow labelled 'therefore p' loops back up.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Hover the contradiction explosion to highlight the exact two claims (r and ¬r) that conflict.

sections.heading: Trivial and Vacuous Proofs
sections.explanation:
Two special-case proof methods are useful inside larger arguments.

  TRIVIAL PROOF: to prove p → q, show q is true outright. Then p → q is true regardless of p.
  VACUOUS PROOF: to prove p → q, show p is false. Then p → q is vacuously true regardless of q.

These are common base cases inside induction and inside case analysis. They look strange in isolation but make perfect logical sense.
examples: Trivial: 'If it is raining, then 1 = 1.' The conclusion is always true, so the implication holds.
Vacuous: 'If 1 + 1 = 3, then your grandma wears combat boots.' The hypothesis is always false, so the implication holds vacuously.
common_mistakes: Calling a proof trivial when really you only handled the easy case. Trivial = conclusion is OUTRIGHT true; not 'easy to see'.
Misusing vacuous proofs to claim absurd conclusions in everyday English. They are formally valid but not informative.

visual_idea.description: Two-row reference table. Row 1: 'Trivial — q is always true ⇒ p → q valid'. Row 2: 'Vacuous — p is always false ⇒ p → q valid'. Each row has an example.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click each row to see how that pattern shows up inside induction base cases.

sections.heading: Proving Biconditional Statements
sections.explanation: A biconditional p ↔ q is logically equivalent to (p → q) ∧ (q → p). To prove p ↔ q, prove BOTH implications. Mathematicians label them (⇒) and (⇐) — or 'necessity' and 'sufficiency' — and write each as a separate sub-proof.
examples: Theorem: 'For integer n, n is odd ⇔ n² is odd.' Proof has two parts: (⇒) direct proof from Section 2; (⇐) contrapositive proof from Section 3.
Theorem: 'A graph is acyclic ⇔ it is a forest.' Two separate proofs are needed — one for each direction.
common_mistakes: Proving only one direction and claiming the biconditional. Both directions are required.
Using one proof method for both directions when one direction would benefit from a different method.

visual_idea.description: Two arrows side by side: a blue ⇒ box ('Assume p, derive q') and a green ⇐ box ('Assume q, derive p'). Both must be filled before the ↔ at the top can be checked off.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Each direction box can independently be expanded into a worked sub-proof, illustrating the two-part structure.

worked_examples.problem: Direct proof: Show that the sum of two even integers is even.
step_by_step_solution: Let m and n be even integers. By definition there exist integers a, b with m = 2a and n = 2b.
Compute m + n = 2a + 2b.
Factor: m + n = 2(a + b).
Since a + b is an integer, m + n has the form 2k, which is the definition of even.
worked_examples.why_it_works: We assumed exactly the hypothesis (both even) and reached exactly the conclusion (sum is even) using only the definition of evenness and basic arithmetic.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing m = 2a and n = 2a (same letter). Different integers need different multipliers.

worked_examples.problem: Contrapositive proof: For integer n, if n² is odd, then n is odd.
step_by_step_solution: We prove the contrapositive: if n is even, then n² is even.
Assume n is even. Then n = 2k for some integer k.
Compute n² = (2k)² = 4k² = 2(2k²).
Since 2k² is an integer, n² has the form 2m, so n² is even.
By contraposition, the original claim holds: n² odd ⇒ n odd.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Proving the contrapositive is logically the same as proving the original, but the contrapositive is much easier here — we never have to factor an odd square.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to mention 'by contraposition' in the closing line. Without that, the reader sees only the contrapositive proven, not the original claim.

worked_examples.problem: Proof by contradiction: Show that √2 is irrational.
step_by_step_solution: Suppose for contradiction that √2 is rational. Then √2 = a/b for integers a, b with b ≠ 0 and the fraction in lowest terms (no common factor > 1).
Square both sides: 2 = a²/b², so a² = 2b².
Hence a² is even, which (by the previous theorem) implies a is even. Write a = 2c.
Substitute: (2c)² = 2b², so 4c² = 2b², so b² = 2c².
Hence b² is even, so b is even.
But a and b are both even — they share the factor 2 — contradicting 'lowest terms'.
The assumption is impossible, so √2 is irrational.
worked_examples.why_it_works: The 'lowest terms' assumption is what gets contradicted. Without it, the argument that both a and b are even would not produce a contradiction.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to assume 'lowest terms'. Every rational has SOME fraction representation; only the lowest-terms version is guaranteed to contradict the both-even conclusion.

worked_examples.problem: Biconditional proof: For integers, n is odd ⇔ n² is odd.
step_by_step_solution: (⇒) Assume n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1. So n² = (2k + 1)² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd.
(⇐) We use the contrapositive proof above: if n is even, then n² is even, so by contraposition n² odd ⇒ n odd.
Both directions hold, so the biconditional is proven.
worked_examples.final_answer: n is odd ⇔ n² is odd. ∎
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each direction may use a different method — direct for (⇒) and contrapositive for (⇐) — whichever is cleaner.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing only the (⇒) direction. A biconditional is incomplete without (⇐).

quick_checks.question: Which proof method assumes the negation of the claim?
quick_checks.explanation: Proof by contradiction assumes ¬p and derives a contradiction.

quick_checks.question: A proof of p ↔ q requires:
choices: Two directions: p → q and q → p
quick_checks.answer: Two directions: p → q and q → p
quick_checks.explanation: p ↔ q ≡ (p → q) ∧ (q → p) — both must be proven.

quick_checks.question: A vacuous proof works by showing the conclusion is always true.
quick_checks.explanation: VACUOUS proofs show the hypothesis is always false. TRIVIAL proofs show the conclusion is always true.

key_takeaways: Theorem (proven), axiom (accepted without proof), lemma (helper), corollary (immediate consequence), conjecture (unproven), proof (justified sequence ending in the claim).
Direct proof: assume p, derive q.
Contrapositive proof: prove ¬q → ¬p, which is equivalent to p → q.
Proof by contradiction: assume ¬claim, derive r ∧ ¬r.
Trivial proof: q is always true. Vacuous proof: p is always false.
Biconditional p ↔ q requires proving both p → q and q → p, possibly with different methods.
summary.next: Next we learn ADVANCED proof strategies: cases, without loss of generality, existence and uniqueness, counterexamples, and forward vs backward reasoning.

lessons.title: Proof Methods and Strategy
lessons.welcome: By now you have direct, contrapositive, and contradiction proofs. But real theorems often require more: splitting the argument into CASES, exploiting symmetry with WITHOUT LOSS OF GENERALITY, constructing or merely demonstrating WITNESSES for existence claims, and proving UNIQUENESS on top of existence. In this lesson you will pick up these strategic moves and learn how to choose the right method for the goal in front of you.
objectives: Construct proofs by cases and verify that the chosen cases are exhaustive.
Use 'without loss of generality' (WLOG) correctly when cases are symmetric.
Distinguish constructive from nonconstructive existence proofs and produce both.
Disprove a universal claim with a single counterexample.
Prove uniqueness (∃!x) by combining an existence proof with a 'any two are equal' argument.
Choose between forward and backward reasoning depending on the structure of the goal.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: How do I prove |n| ≥ 0 for every integer when |n| is defined piecewise?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: Proof by CASES. Handle each branch of the definition. Case 1: n ≥ 0, then |n| = n ≥ 0. Case 2: n < 0, then |n| = −n > 0. Both cases together cover every integer.

storytelling.speaker: Student
storytelling.text: And how do I show that some irrational raised to an irrational power is rational?

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: NONCONSTRUCTIVE existence. Look at √2^√2. If it is rational, take x = y = √2 — done. If it is irrational, take x = √2^√2 and y = √2; then x^y = 2, rational. Either way two such numbers exist — without ever telling you which case is the actual one.

storytelling.speaker: Professor
storytelling.text: It feels strange but it is fully rigorous. The theorem says 'there exist' — we proved that two specific candidates can not both fail.

sections.heading: Proof by Cases
sections.explanation:
When the hypothesis splits naturally into a finite number of EXHAUSTIVE possibilities p₁ ∨ p₂ ∨ ⋯ ∨ pₙ, prove the conclusion in each case separately. Crucially, the cases must COVER every possibility — missing one case invalidates the proof.

  Skeleton:
  1. 'Case 1: p₁. … so q.'
  2. 'Case 2: p₂. … so q.'
  …
  3. 'Since the cases are exhaustive, q in every case. ∎'

Common case-splits: by parity (even/odd), by sign (positive/zero/negative), by comparison (<, =, >), or by the branches of a piecewise definition.
examples: Theorem: 'For every integer n, n² ≥ n.' Cases: n ≥ 1 ⇒ n² = n·n ≥ n. n = 0 ⇒ 0 ≥ 0. n ≤ −1 ⇒ n² ≥ 1 > 0 ≥ n. Cases exhaust ℤ. ∎
Theorem: '|x · y| = |x| · |y| for real x, y.' Cases by signs of x and y.
common_mistakes: Cases that do not cover all possibilities (e.g., considering positive and negative but forgetting zero).
Cases that overlap and prove the same thing twice — not wrong but inefficient.

visual_idea.description: A diamond at the top splitting into branches, one per case. Each branch holds a sub-proof and ends in the conclusion. The branches reunite at a final box labeled 'q in every case'.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Toggle one of the cases off; the page warns 'cases are no longer exhaustive — proof is incomplete'.

sections.heading: Without Loss of Generality (WLOG)
sections.explanation:
When two or more cases are STRUCTURALLY IDENTICAL except for relabeling, prove one and assert the other 'without loss of generality'. The phrase signals to the reader: 'this argument works for the symmetric case verbatim, swapping labels'.

Use WLOG only when the cases are TRULY symmetric. Abusing WLOG to skip cases that are merely similar is a common mistake.
examples: Theorem: 'If both x · y and x + y are even, then both x and y are even.' Contrapositive: assume not both x, y even. WLOG x is odd (otherwise swap labels). Then in two sub-cases (y even, y odd), one of x · y, x + y comes out odd. ∎
Theorem: '|x − y| = |y − x|.' WLOG x ≥ y; the other case is identical by swap.
common_mistakes: Using WLOG when cases are not actually symmetric. If swapping labels changes the structure of the argument, WLOG does not apply.
Skipping the explicit 'without loss of generality, x is …' phrase. The reader needs to know which label you fixed.

visual_idea.description: Two side-by-side boxes representing the cases. A double-headed swap arrow connects them, labeled 'symmetric'. Above both is a single proof box, labeled 'one proof covers both via WLOG'.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click the swap arrow to highlight which labels are exchanged when the symmetry is invoked.

sections.heading: Existence Proofs: Constructive vs Nonconstructive
sections.explanation:
To prove ∃x P(x), you need to demonstrate that at least one element makes P true. Two flavors:

  CONSTRUCTIVE — explicitly produce a witness c with P(c). The reader can see the c.
  NONCONSTRUCTIVE — prove that some witness must exist WITHOUT producing it. Often via case analysis or contradiction.

Constructive proofs are more informative when they are available; nonconstructive proofs are sometimes the only option.
examples: Constructive: 'There exists a positive integer expressible as a sum of two cubes in two different ways.' 1729 = 1³ + 12³ = 9³ + 10³. ∎

Nonconstructive: 'There exist irrationals x, y with x^y rational.' Consider √2^√2: if rational, take x = y = √2; if irrational, take x = √2^√2 and y = √2, so x^y = (√2^√2)^√2 = √2² = 2. Either way x and y exist. ∎
common_mistakes: Claiming constructive existence without checking the candidate actually satisfies P.
Treating nonconstructive proofs as somehow weaker. They are fully rigorous — just less informative.

visual_idea.description: Two cards. Constructive: a labelled witness c framed in green with 'P(c) ✓' beside it. Nonconstructive: a question-marked '?' and two alternative paths both leading to 'witness exists' without revealing which path is real.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click the constructive card to type your own witness and have the page check P(c). The nonconstructive card shows the case-split argument step by step.

sections.heading: Counterexamples and Nonexistence Proofs
sections.explanation:
To DISPROVE a universal claim ∀x P(x), exhibit ONE element c with ¬P(c). That c is a COUNTEREXAMPLE. A single counterexample is decisive — no need to check anything else.

To prove a NONEXISTENCE claim ¬∃x P(x), use the equivalent universal ∀x ¬P(x) and apply any universal proof method (typically contradiction or contraposition).
examples: Disproof: 'Every positive integer is the sum of squares of three integers.' Counterexample: n = 7 cannot be written that way (try all triples; the maximum each square can contribute is bounded).
Disproof: 'Every prime is odd.' Counterexample: 2.
Nonexistence: 'No integer satisfies n² = 2.' Equivalent to ∀n (n² ≠ 2); easy to verify by case analysis.
common_mistakes: Trying to disprove a universal by 'most cases fail'. ONE counterexample is required and ONE counterexample is sufficient.
Confusing nonexistence proofs with universal proofs. They are the same task in different clothing.

visual_idea.description: A grid of domain elements. Hovering shows P(x) for each. The first red cell encountered is highlighted with a 'counterexample!' banner; the rest of the grid greys out — emphasizing that one is enough.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Type your own predicate; click 'find counterexample' and the page sweeps the grid until the first failure.

sections.heading: Uniqueness Proofs
sections.explanation:
Some theorems claim BOTH existence and uniqueness, written ∃!x P(x). A uniqueness proof has TWO halves:

  EXISTENCE: produce some x with P(x) (constructive or nonconstructive).
  UNIQUENESS: show that any two witnesses are equal — i.e., assume P(x) and P(y), then derive x = y.

Skipping either half is a common mistake.
examples: Theorem: 'For real a ≠ 0, b, the equation ax + b = 0 has a unique real solution.' Existence: x = −b/a satisfies the equation. Uniqueness: if as + b = 0 too, then ar = as where r = −b/a; subtract and divide by a ≠ 0 to get s = r. ∎

Theorem: 'Every nonempty set of positive integers has a unique smallest element.' Existence by well-ordering principle; uniqueness because two 'smallest' elements would each be ≤ the other, hence equal.
common_mistakes: Proving only existence and assuming uniqueness is automatic. It is not.
In the uniqueness step, taking x = y as a starting assumption instead of as the conclusion.

visual_idea.description: Two boxes side by side. Left: 'Existence — produce x with P(x)'. Right: 'Uniqueness — assume P(x) and P(y), derive x = y'. Both boxes must be checked off before the ∃! claim above can be marked complete.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Click each half independently to expand into the worked sub-proof.

sections.heading: Proof Strategy: Forward, Backward, and Choosing a Method
sections.explanation:
A METHOD is the kind of proof (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, …). A STRATEGY is the direction in which you build the argument.

  FORWARD reasoning starts from the hypothesis and derives consequences until reaching the conclusion. Natural for direct proofs.
  BACKWARD reasoning starts from the conclusion, asks 'what would suffice to prove this?', and walks back until reaching something already known. Useful for inequalities, game-theory strategies, and complex goals.

Most real proofs combine forward and backward reasoning, meeting somewhere in the middle.

  STRATEGY LADDER for choosing a method:
  1. Try DIRECT proof.
  2. If direct is messy, try CONTRAPOSITION.
  3. If neither works, try CONTRADICTION.
  4. If the hypothesis splits, use CASES.
  5. For ∃-claims, try CONSTRUCTIVE; if that fails, NONCONSTRUCTIVE.
  6. To disprove a ∀-claim, hunt for a COUNTEREXAMPLE.
examples: Backward: 'In a game removing 1, 2, or 3 stones from 15, the first player wins.' Work backward: a player faced with 4 stones must leave a losing position. Multiples of 4 are losing positions. 15 mod 4 = 3, so the first player removes 3 stones, leaves 12 (multiple of 4), and the opponent is doomed.
Forward + backward meet-in-the-middle: prove an inequality by simultaneously simplifying both sides until they match.
common_mistakes: Refusing to try backward reasoning because 'proofs go forward'. Backward reasoning is a planning tool — your final write-up can still flow forward.
Sticking to one method when the goal clearly suggests another (e.g., trying direct proof on a nonexistence claim).

visual_idea.description: A decision tree starting with 'What is the goal?' Branches by goal shape (p → q, ∃x, ∀x, ¬∃x, ∃!x) lead to recommended methods. Below each method leaf, an arrow indicates the natural direction (forward or backward) for that style.
visual_idea.interactive_hint: Type your goal; the page traces the recommended branch and highlights the suggested method and direction.

worked_examples.problem: Proof by cases: For every integer n, n² ≥ n.
step_by_step_solution: Case 1: n ≥ 1. Then n² = n · n ≥ n · 1 = n.
Case 2: n = 0. Then n² = 0 = n.
Case 3: n ≤ −1. Then n² ≥ 1 > 0 > n.
Cases exhaust ℤ, so n² ≥ n for every integer.
worked_examples.why_it_works: Each case handles a structurally different sign or comparison. Their union is all of ℤ.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Skipping the n = 0 case. Boundary cases are easy to miss but essential for exhaustiveness.

worked_examples.problem: WLOG: If both x · y and x + y are even, then both x and y are even.
step_by_step_solution: Prove the contrapositive: if x and y are not both even, then x · y is odd OR x + y is odd.
Assume not both even. WLOG x is odd (otherwise relabel). Write x = 2m + 1.
Case A: y is even. y = 2n. Then x + y = (2m + 1) + 2n = 2(m + n) + 1 is odd.
Case B: y is odd. y = 2n + 1. Then x · y = (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 is odd.
In either case, one of x · y, x + y is odd. By contraposition, the original holds.
worked_examples.final_answer: Both x and y must be even. ∎
worked_examples.why_it_works: WLOG halves the work because the argument is symmetric in x and y. The two sub-cases inside (y even, y odd) exhaust the remaining possibilities.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting to consider y odd inside the WLOG branch. WLOG handles symmetry between x and y, but you still need to handle all cases for y.

worked_examples.problem: Constructive existence: There is a positive integer expressible as a sum of two cubes in two different ways.
step_by_step_solution: Two distinct representations. Done.
worked_examples.why_it_works: We exhibited an explicit witness and verified P(witness).
worked_examples.common_mistake: Listing the witness without verifying both representations give the same value.

step_by_step_solution: Find one prime that is even.
2 is prime (its only positive divisors are 1 and 2).
2 is even.
So 2 is a counterexample.
worked_examples.final_answer: 2 is a counterexample. The claim is false. ∎
worked_examples.why_it_works: A single counterexample is decisive against a universal claim.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Pretending you need to check more cases. One is enough.

worked_examples.problem: Uniqueness: For real a ≠ 0, b, the equation ax + b = 0 has a unique real solution.
step_by_step_solution: EXISTENCE: x = −b/a satisfies the equation, since a(−b/a) + b = −b + b = 0.
UNIQUENESS: suppose s also satisfies as + b = 0. Then a(−b/a) + b = as + b, so a(−b/a) = as.
Subtract b from both sides: a(−b/a) = as. Divide by a ≠ 0: −b/a = s.
So s = −b/a, the same as the witness. Therefore the solution is unique.
worked_examples.why_it_works: The existence half produces a witness; the uniqueness half uses a ≠ 0 to cancel and conclude any two witnesses are equal.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Forgetting the uniqueness step. Existence alone allows for the possibility of multiple solutions.

quick_checks.question: To disprove 'every prime is odd', the cleanest argument is:
choices: A direct proof of the negation
quick_checks.explanation: A single counterexample disproves a universal claim.

quick_checks.question: A nonconstructive existence proof:
choices: Proves a witness must exist without naming it.
quick_checks.answer: Proves a witness must exist without naming it.
quick_checks.explanation: It establishes existence (often via case analysis or contradiction) without exhibiting a specific c.

quick_checks.question: WLOG can be used whenever two cases look 'similar'.
quick_checks.explanation: WLOG requires TRUE structural symmetry — the argument must transfer verbatim by swapping labels.

key_takeaways: Proof by cases requires that the cases be EXHAUSTIVE.
WLOG is valid only when cases are structurally symmetric.
Constructive existence: produce a witness. Nonconstructive: prove one must exist without producing it.
A single counterexample disproves a universal claim.
Uniqueness proofs have two halves: existence + 'any two witnesses are equal'.
Strategy ladder: direct → contrapositive → contradiction → cases → constructive ∃ → nonconstructive ∃ → counterexample for ¬∀.
Forward reasoning grows the known; backward reasoning grows the goal — combine them.
summary.next: You now have the full Module 3 toolkit. Move to the Module 3 exercises page to practice rules of inference, proof methods, and proof strategy on a wide mix of problems.

exercises.title: Module 3 Exercises — Proofs
exercises.description: Practice problems for Module 3: rules of inference, formal proofs, the four cornerstone proof methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, vacuous/trivial), advanced strategies (cases, WLOG, existence, uniqueness, counterexamples), and proof-direction choices. MCQ, true/false, short answer, step-by-step, exam-style, and randomized templates.

questions.question: From premises 'If it rains the grass is wet' and 'It is raining', conclude:
questions.answer: The grass is wet.
questions.explanation: Modus Ponens: p, p → q ⊢ q.

questions.question: From premises 'If she studies, she passes' and 'She did not pass', conclude:
questions.answer: She did not study.
questions.explanation: Modus Tollens: ¬q, p → q ⊢ ¬p.

questions.question: Which is INVALID?
questions.answer: Affirming the Consequent
questions.explanation: From p → q and q, you cannot conclude p — q might hold for other reasons.

questions.question: Existential Instantiation introduces a constant that:
choices: Must equal a named element of the domain.
Can be any previously used name.
Must be a NEW name not used elsewhere.
Need not exist if the domain is empty.
questions.answer: Must be a NEW name not used elsewhere.
questions.explanation: EI's witness is unknown; reusing a name would assert facts about a specific known element.

questions.question: Best method to prove 'if n² is odd, then n is odd':
questions.answer: Contrapositive
questions.explanation: Direct proof would require factoring an odd square. Contrapositive (assume n even, derive n² even) is cleaner.

questions.question: A proof by contradiction of claim p:
choices: Assumes p and derives a contradiction.
questions.answer: Assumes ¬p and derives a contradiction.
questions.explanation: If ¬p leads to absurdity, ¬p must be false, so p is true.

questions.question: Which claim requires both an existence proof AND a uniqueness proof?
questions.answer: ∃!x P(x)
questions.explanation: The 'unique' qualifier needs uniqueness in addition to existence.

questions.question: WLOG is appropriate when:
choices: The omitted case is similar by symmetry.
You forgot to handle the case.
The case is too long to write.
questions.answer: The omitted case is similar by symmetry.
questions.explanation: WLOG is a shortcut for 'the same argument works for the symmetric case verbatim by relabelling'.

questions.question: An argument is sound iff it is valid AND has all true premises.
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: Validity is about form; soundness adds true premises.

questions.question: Resolution is the rule [p ∨ q, ¬p ∨ r] ⊢ q ∨ r.
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: It cancels p with ¬p and disjoins the remaining literals.

questions.question: p → q is logically equivalent to ¬q → ¬p.
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: This is the contrapositive equivalence.

questions.question: Universal Generalization can be applied to any element you have already named in a proof.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: UG requires the element to be ARBITRARY — typically introduced as 'let c be arbitrary'.

questions.question: A trivial proof of p → q shows that p is always false.
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: That is a VACUOUS proof. Trivial proofs show q is always true.

questions.question: Two counterexamples are needed to disprove ∀x P(x).
questions.answer: False
questions.explanation: One counterexample suffices.

questions.question: Proving ∃!x P(x) requires showing both existence AND that any two witnesses are equal.
questions.answer: True
questions.explanation: Existence + uniqueness; both halves are needed.

questions.question: Define 'valid argument' formally.
questions.answer: An argument with premises p₁, …, pₙ and conclusion q is valid iff (p₁ ∧ ⋯ ∧ pₙ) → q is a tautology — equivalently, every truth assignment that makes all premises true also makes q true.
questions.explanation: Validity is about form; a valid argument with false premises is still valid (just not sound).

questions.question: Why does Existential Instantiation require a fresh constant?
questions.answer: Because the witness from ∃x P(x) is unknown. Reusing an existing name would assert facts about a specific known element rather than about an unknown witness.
questions.explanation: Fresh names prevent illegal cross-references with previously named objects.

questions.question: Give a direct proof: the square of any odd integer is odd.
questions.answer: Let n be odd. Then n = 2k + 1 for some integer k. So n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which has the form 2r + 1 — odd. ∎
questions.explanation: Direct application of the definition of odd, plus algebra.

questions.question: Why is the strategy 'direct → contrapositive → contradiction' a sensible default order?
questions.answer: Direct proofs are usually most informative when they work. Contraposition is a single re-framing that often makes a hard hypothesis easier. Contradiction is the most general but often hides why the result is true — try it last.
questions.explanation: Easier-and-more-informative-first.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'cases must be exhaustive' and 'cases must be disjoint'?
questions.answer: Cases must be exhaustive — every possibility must fall into at least one case. Cases need NOT be disjoint; overlapping cases are allowed (just less efficient). Missing a case invalidates a proof; overlap merely repeats work.
questions.explanation: Exhaustiveness is required; disjointness is a stylistic preference.

questions.question: Use rules of inference to show that the hypotheses 'If it does not rain or it is not foggy, then the sailing race is held and the demo continues', 'If the race is held, the trophy is awarded', and 'The trophy was not awarded' imply 'It rained'.
questions.answer:
Let r, f, s, d, t denote rain, fog, race held, demo, trophy.
1. (¬r ∨ ¬f) → (s ∧ d)   premise
2. s → t                  premise
3. ¬t                     premise
4. ¬s                     MT (2, 3)
5. ¬s ∨ ¬d                Addition (4)
6. ¬(s ∧ d)               De Morgan (5)
7. ¬(¬r ∨ ¬f)             MT (1, 6)
8. r ∧ f                  De Morgan + double negation (7)
9. r                      Simplification (8)
questions.explanation: Chain of MT, Addition, De Morgan, MT, Simplification.

questions.question: Use a direct proof to show that the product of two rational numbers is rational.
questions.answer:
Let r and s be rational. Then there exist integers p, q, t, u with q ≠ 0, u ≠ 0 such that r = p/q and s = t/u.
Compute r·s = (p/q)·(t/u) = (pt)/(qu).
Since pt is an integer and qu is a non-zero integer, r·s is rational. ∎
questions.explanation: Direct application of the definition of rational, plus integer arithmetic.

questions.question: Use proof by contraposition: if x + y ≥ 2 (real x, y), then x ≥ 1 or y ≥ 1.
questions.answer:
Contrapositive: if NOT (x ≥ 1 ∨ y ≥ 1), then NOT (x + y ≥ 2).
Assume x < 1 AND y < 1. Then x + y < 1 + 1 = 2, so x + y < 2.
By contraposition, x + y ≥ 2 implies x ≥ 1 or y ≥ 1. ∎
questions.explanation: Contrapositive turns a tricky disjunctive conclusion into a clean conjunctive hypothesis.

questions.question: Show by cases: for every integer n, n² + n is even.
questions.answer:
Case 1: n is even. Then n = 2k, so n² + n = 4k² + 2k = 2(2k² + k), even.
Case 2: n is odd. Then n = 2k + 1, so n² + n = (4k² + 4k + 1) + (2k + 1) = 4k² + 6k + 2 = 2(2k² + 3k + 1), even.
Cases exhaust ℤ. ∎
questions.explanation: Parity case-split — the standard tool for integer claims.

questions.question: For each argument decide whether the rule used is Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, Hypothetical Syllogism, or Disjunctive Syllogism: (a) 'If it snows, the school closes. The school is open. Therefore it did not snow.' (b) 'If I go swimming, I will get sunburned. I went swimming. Therefore I got sunburned.' (c) 'Either it is raining or it is sunny. It is not raining. Therefore it is sunny.' (d) 'If A then B. If B then C. Therefore if A then C.'
questions.answer: (a) MT. (b) MP. (c) DS. (d) HS.
questions.explanation: Each pattern matches one of the four named rules exactly.

questions.question: Show that ∀x (P(x) ∨ Q(x)), ∀x (¬Q(x) ∨ S(x)), ∀x (R(x) → ¬S(x)), and ∃x ¬P(x) imply ∃x ¬R(x).
questions.answer:
1. ∃x ¬P(x)                 premise
2. ¬P(c)                    EI (1) — c fresh
3. P(c) ∨ Q(c)              UI on first premise
4. Q(c)                     DS (2, 3)
5. ¬Q(c) ∨ S(c)             UI on second premise
6. S(c)                     DS (4 with ¬¬Q(c) ≡ Q(c) and 5)
7. R(c) → ¬S(c)             UI on third premise
8. ¬R(c)                    MT (6, 7)
9. ∃x ¬R(x)                 EG (8)
questions.explanation: EI gives a witness; UI specializes the universals; DS, MT, and EG do the rest.

questions.question: Show that 'If you send me an email, I will finish the program', 'If you do not send me an email, I will go to bed early', and 'If I go to bed early, I will wake up refreshed' imply 'If I do not finish the program, I will wake up refreshed'.
questions.answer:
Let e, p, b, w denote email, program, bed early, wake refreshed.
1. e → p                  premise
2. ¬e → b                 premise
3. b → w                  premise
4. ¬p → ¬e                contrapositive of (1)
5. ¬e → w                 HS (2, 3)
6. ¬p → w                 HS (4, 5). ∎
questions.explanation: Chain HS twice, using the contrapositive of (1) to bridge ¬p back to ¬e.

questions.question: Use a proof by contradiction to show that there is no largest prime.
questions.answer:
Suppose there is a largest prime p. Then the primes are 2, 3, 5, …, p.
Form r = 2 · 3 · 5 · ⋯ · p + 1.
Each known prime divides r − 1, so leaves remainder 1 when dividing r — none divide r.
Therefore r is either prime itself (a new prime greater than p) or has a prime factor not in our list.
Either case contradicts the assumption that p was the largest prime. ∎
questions.explanation: Classical Euclid argument; the contradiction is 'p was largest' vs 'there is a larger prime'.

questions.question: Show that the equation a + b = b + a is unique up to evaluation: prove that for any reals a, b, there is a unique real c with c = a + b.
questions.answer:
Existence: c = a + b satisfies c = a + b.
Uniqueness: if c' is another real with c' = a + b, then c = a + b = c', so c = c'.
∃! holds. ∎
questions.explanation: Trivially structured uniqueness proof — illustrates the two-half pattern.

questions.template: From premises {PREMISE1} and {PREMISE2}, what valid conclusion follows by {RULE}?
questions.instructions: Pick a (PREMISE1, PREMISE2, RULE) triple where the rule actually applies; otherwise re-roll. Identify the conclusion.
questions.example_realization: Realization: p → q, p, MP. Conclusion: q.
questions.explanation: Random drill on which two premises feed which rule.

questions.template: Choose the best proof method for: '{CLAIM}'.

CLAIM: If n² is even, then n is even.
There exist irrationals x, y with x^y rational.
For every integer n, n² + n is even.
Every prime greater than 2 is odd.

questions.instructions: Match each claim to the cleanest method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, cases, constructive ∃, nonconstructive ∃).
questions.example_realization: Realization: 'If n² is even, then n is even.' Best method: contrapositive.
questions.explanation: Method selection drill builds strategic taste.

questions.template: Identify whether the following argument is VALID or a FALLACY: '{ARGUMENT}'.

ARGUMENT: If it rains the road is wet. The road is wet. Therefore it is raining.
If it rains the road is wet. It is not raining. Therefore the road is not wet.
If it rains the road is wet. It is raining. Therefore the road is wet.
If it rains the road is wet. The road is not wet. Therefore it is not raining.
Either you study or you fail. You did not study. Therefore you failed.

questions.instructions: Check the form: MP and MT are valid; affirming-the-consequent and denying-the-antecedent are fallacies; DS is valid.
questions.example_realization: Realization: 'If it rains the road is wet. The road is wet. Therefore it is raining.' This is affirming the consequent — FALLACY.
questions.explanation: Repeated drill removes the most common reasoning errors.

questions.template: Translate the proof skeleton: prove '{CLAIM}' using {METHOD}. Provide the first three lines of the proof.

the product of two even integers is even
the square of any integer is non-negative
if a divides b and b divides c, then a divides c

questions.instructions: Open with 'Assume …', name the integers, apply the relevant definition, and stop after three lines.
questions.example_realization: Realization: claim 'sum of two odd integers is even', METHOD direct. Lines: 'Let m, n be odd. Then m = 2a + 1 and n = 2b + 1 for integers a, b. Compute m + n = 2(a + b + 1).'
